title: Microstructure and mechanical properties of laser welded dissimilar materials joints between CLF-1 and ITER-grade 316LN steels for nuclear fusion reactor
abstract: Abstract The structural integrity of the Test Blanket Module (TBM) in the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) depends on robust dissimilar joints between China low-activation ferritic (CLF-1) steel and ITER-grade 316LN (316LN-IG) austenitic stainless steel. In this study, CLF-1/316LN-IG dissimilar steel joints were fabricated by laser welding, and the microstructural evolution in the weld metal (WM) and heat-affected zone (HAZ) was systematically investigated by multiscale characterization combined with mechanical testing, with particular emphasis on correlating microstructure with mechanical performance. The WM consists of columnar austenitic dendrites and lath martensite, while the HAZ of CLF-1 is distinguished by the presence of intragranular TaC carbides and intergranular (Cr, W) 23 C 6  carbides. The welded joint exhibited excellent overall tensile performance, with an ultimate tensile strength of 619.0 MPa, comparable to that of 316LN-IG, a yield strength of 365.8 MPa, 11.5% higher than 316LN-IG, and the total elongation reaches 45.5%, 70.4% higher than CLF-1. Tensile fracture occurs in the base material far from the weld. The impact absorbed energy of the weld is intermediate between those of CLF-1 and 316LN-IG steel. The enhancement of strength is attributed to the high dislocation density in the lath martensite within the WM, and to the strengthening effect of nanoscale carbides in the CLF-1 HAZ. Moreover, first-principles and thermodynamic calculations elucidate the phase stability of TaC and (Cr, W) 23 C 6 , providing a fundamental basis for the structural and materials design of TBM components.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: With the continuous growth of global energy demand, fossil fuels remain dominant and contribute to substantial carbon dioxide emissions. Consequently, low-carbon energy supply has become an urgent priority [ 1 ,  2 ]. Nuclear energy, characterized by its high energy density and near-zero emissions during operation, is regarded as a promising solution [ 3 ]. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) project, currently the largest fusion experimental facility, aims to achieve approximately a tenfold power amplification to validate the feasibility of nuclear fusion as a scalable clean energy source [ 4 ,  5 ]. Test Blanket Module (TBM), as a critical component, is responsible for verifying tritium breeding and the efficient extraction of high-quality thermal energy. The manufacturing process of TBM inevitably involves extensive dissimilar metal welding, particularly between the China low-activation ferritic (CLF-1) steel and ITER-grade 316LN (316LN-IG) austenitic stainless steel [ 6 ,  7 ]. However, significant disparities in thermal expansion coefficients, strength, and microstructural evolution behavior during welding thermal cycles render dissimilar steel welding highly susceptible to microstructural distribution inhomogeneity in the weld, inconsistent properties across different regions, and increased defect susceptibility. Consequently, the process of welding dissimilar steels poses considerable technical challenges.

Extensive studies have explored dissimilar welding between reduced activation ferritic/martensitic (RAFM) steel and 316L austenitic stainless steel using various welding processes, including laser welding [ 8 ], electron beam welding [ 9 ], tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding [ 10 ] and friction stir welding [ 11 ]. Shi et al. [ 12 ] successfully produced RAFM/316L weld joints by laser welding, achieving a weld Charpy impact energy of up to 130 J, with the weld metal (WM) exhibiting ductile fracture and good toughness. Liu et al. [ 13 ] joined RAFM steel to 316L stainless steel by electron beam welding, the resulting welds were free of defects, and the fusion zone consisted of martensite, austenite and ferrite. The welded joints exhibited ultimate tensile strength and yield strength superior to those of both base materials (BMs), although their elongation was significantly reduced. Yoon et al. [ 14 ] fabricated 12 mm-thick RAFM/316L joints using multi-pass TIG welding, and after post-weld heat treatment, the maximum impact energy of the welds reached 99 J. He et al. [ 15 ] investigated microstructure and mechanical properties of RAFM/316L dissimilar joints produced by friction stir welding, finding that at −40 °C the heat-affected zone (HAZ) on the RAFM side exhibited the lowest impact toughness and brittle fracture, whereas all other regions failed in a ductile manner. However, TIG welding generally requires high heat input and generates a wide HAZ, which exacerbates distortion and degrades the impact toughness of the joint. In the fabrication of large components, friction stir welding is constrained by tool length and is not suitable for thick-section plates, while electron beam welding must be carried out in vacuum, imposing severe limitations on component size and workspace. Consequently, there is a strong need for a welding technique that combines high energy density, low overall heat input, a narrow HAZ, and good process adaptability. Owing to its high energy density, high processing speed, and small HAZ, laser welding is regarded as a promising technology for joining dissimilar and thick-walled nuclear structural materials [ 16 ,  17 ].

316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel, an ITER-grade austenitic alloy, has been designated as the austenitic counterpart welded to RAFM steels in TBM components for the ITER project [ 18 ]. Nevertheless, 316LN-IG differs significantly from the extensively studied 316L stainless steel with regard to alloy design and impurity control. In 316LN-IG steel, the contents of activation-relevant trace elements such as cobalt and niobium, as well as residual elements such as boron that promote helium generation, are stringently restricted [ 19 ]. Concurrently, the nitrogen content is tightly controlled to meet fusion-relevant performance and weldability requirements [ 18 ,  20 ]. These compositional disparities give rise to distinct microstructural features. 316L stainless steel exhibits a duplex microstructure consisting of austenite with a small fraction of ferrite [ 21 ,  22 ], whereas 316LN-IG stainless steel shows a fully austenitic structure. In accordance with the findings of preceding research, these ostensibly trivial compositional adjustments have the potential to influence the solidification process of the molten pool during laser welding, the microstructure of the welded joint, and the joint's performance [ 23 ,  24 ]. Consequently, a systematic investigation into the laser welding behavior of CLF-1 steel in combination with 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel is required.

In this study, a systematic investigation was conducted on dissimilar laser-welded joints between CLF-1 steel and 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel, both of which are utilized as structural materials in TBM components of fusion reactors. The feasibility and engineering relevance of this joining strategy are assessed by combining multiscale microstructural characterization with mechanical testing. The present study focuses on the microstructural evolution of the WM and the HAZ in the dissimilar joint. It systematically links local microstructural features to the macroscopic mechanical response. In addition, first-principles and thermodynamic calculations are utilized to elucidate the phase stability of TaC and (Cr, W) 23 C 6  carbides in the HAZ on the CLF-1 side. The results of this study provide a process-property benchmark for CLF-1/316LN-IG dissimilar welds in critical TBM regions and offer useful guidance for subsequent structural material selection and weld design optimization.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs:
CLF-1 steel and 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel plates with a thickness of 10 mm were used in the present study. Specifically, the CLF-1 steel was quenched at 980 °C for 1 h and then tempered at 740 °C for 2 h. The 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel was in the solid-solution tempered state. The chemical composition of CLF-1 steel and 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel is listed in Table  1 . The microstructure of the CLF-1 steel is tempered martensite. The microstructure of the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel is restricted to full austenitic, which is considered for the magnetic and cryogenic service conditions.

sections.heading: Welding process
paragraphs: The as-received CLF-1 steel plate and 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel plate were sliced into sheets measuring 120 mm × 60 mm × 10 mm in size by wire electric discharge machining (EDM) for laser welding experiments. Before the laser welding experiment, the welding surface was milled to ensure there were no gaps on the butt joint, and other surfaces were and blasted to clean the surface oxide. Acetone was used to clean the surface, and then the BMs were fixed on the clamping platform with a 0 mm gap to ensure adequate restraint.

A high-power double-mode continuous wave fiber laser (IPG YLS-30000) equipment with a maximum output power of 30 kW was applied for the laser welding experiments. The wavelength of the laser was 1070 nm, with a focused spot diameter of 600 μm. A laser welding head was mounted on a 6-axis KUKA robot. The angle between the laser beam and the vertical direction of the workpieces was set as 10° to avoid laser reflection to damage the laser head. A schematic of the laser welding set-up is shown in Fig.  1 a. The welding process was carried out vertically to the rolling direction of the CLF-1 steel. Nitrogen gas was used as the shielding gas, as it is widely adopted for welding 316LN-type austenitic stainless steels and provides reliable protection against oxidation under the present laser welding conditions. Previous research optimized laser process parameters for joining CLF-1/316LN-IG dissimilar steels using response surface methodology, with the obtained optimized processing parameters shown in Table  2 . The detailed optimization process is referred to [ 27 ]. sections.heading: Metallography and hardness measurements
paragraphs: After welding, the as-welded specimens were first sampled via wire EDM for metallographic examination and microhardness testing. Subsequently, the metallographic and microhardness testing specimens underwent sequential grinding and polishing, followed by etching with Villella reagent (1 g picric acid + 10 ml HCl + 100 ml alcohol) for approximately 10 s. Macroscopic morphology of the welded specimens was observed using an EasyZoom5 3D deep-field microscope. Microstructure analysis was performed using a Zeiss Gemini SEM 300 scanning electron microscope (SEM) combined with electron back scatter diffraction (EBSD) technology. Microstructure and dislocation distribution were characterized using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, Thermo Scientific Talos F200X). TEM specimens were prepared using a focused ion beam-scanning electron microscope (Thermo Scientific Scios 2). Microhardness distributions were measured at the mid-cross-section of the welded joint using an HVS-1000Z Vickers hardness tester. Test conditions included a load of 300 g, a dwell time of 10 s, and an indentation spacing of 0.1 mm.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties testing
paragraphs: Tensile and Charpy impact tests were conducted on the BMs and weld specimens, respectively. Tensile testing was performed at room temperature using a C45.105EY electronic universal testing machine equipped with a Red Box-HH non-contact video extensometer, with specimens prepared and tested according to ASTM E8/E8M-2016a. Impact toughness was tested at room temperature using the pendulum-type Charpy V-notch method on a ZBC2752-D impact testing machine. Specimens were prepared and tested according to ASTM E23-02a, with the V-notch located at the weld center. To minimize testing uncertainty, three specimens were tested for tensile and Charpy impact tests. All specimens were extracted from the BMs and welded samples using wire EDM. The major axis of each specimen type was perpendicular to the welding direction. Specimen dimensions and sampling locations are shown in Fig.  1 b.

sections.heading: First-principles calculation
paragraphs: First-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) to evaluate the formation enthalpies and elastic moduli of M 23 C 6  and MX carbides. All calculations were conducted using idealized periodic crystal models, and the results are intended primarily for comparative assessment of candidate carbide phases. The space group of M 23 C 6  is Fm-3m, with 116 atoms per cell. The space group of MX is Fm-3m, with 8 atoms per cell. The electronic exchange–correlation interaction was described by the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA), and valence electron–ion interactions were treated using the projected augmented wave (PAW) method. Formation enthalpies were calculated from the DFT total energies of the compounds relative to the energies of the constituent reference states. Elastic constants were obtained by applying small finite strains to the equilibrium cell and fitting the resulting stress–strain relations to extract the stiffness tensor [ 28 ,  29 ]. The bulk, shear and Young’s moduli were then derived from the aforementioned data, and an isotropic aggregate modulus was obtained using the Voigt–Reuss–Hill averaging scheme.

sections.heading: Macrostructure
paragraphs: Figure  2  shows the cross-sectional morphology and elemental distribution map of the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint. The cross-sectional morphology reveals good metallurgical bonding between the two materials, with no macro defects such as porosity or cracks present in the welded joint. Simultaneously, the microstructure at the welded joint can be divided into four distinct sub-regions: the base material of CLF-1 steel (CLF-1 BM), the HAZ of CLF-1 steel (CLF-1 HAZ), the WM, and the base material of 316LN-IG steel (316LN-IG BM). Fig. 2 Cross-section morphology and elements distribution of CLF-1/316LN-IG dissimilar steels laser welded joint:  a  low-magnification cross-section of the laser welded joint showing the CLF-1 BM, CLF-1 HAZ, WM and 316LN-IG BM,  b  EDS elemental maps acquired from the mid-thickness region of the joint, revealing the spatial distribution of Fe, Cr, Mn, Mo and Ni,  c  corresponding EDS line-scan profiles across the mid-thickness region of the joint, showing the compositional gradients of Fe, Cr, Mn, Mo and Ni

Macroscopic observation (Fig.  2 a) reveals pronounced asymmetry in the dissimilar weld joint. A broad HAZ is present on the CLF-1 steel side, whereas no distinct HAZ is observed on the 316LN-IG stainless steel side. Energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) mapping scans reveal the spatial distribution of representative alloying elements (Fe, Cr, Mn, Mo, and Ni), as shown in Fig.  2 b. Results indicate composition dilution of the two dissimilar materials within the weld, with pronounced composition gradients observed at both fusion interfaces. Typical linear scans obtained along the red arrow path in Fig.  2 a, covering the CLF-1 BM, CLF-1 HAZ, WM, and 316LN-IG BM, reveal continuous gradient changes in representative alloying elements and indicate the weld width (Fig.  2 c). Furthermore, the steep changes in elemental content near the fusion interface are consistent with limited solid-state diffusion during thermal cycling [ 30 ]. Overall, the weld zone exhibits uniform geometry, good surface quality, and a continuous fusion interface, indicating that a sound dissimilar steel joint of CLF-1/316LN-IG was successfully produced by laser welding.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: Figure  3  displays the distributions of the main alloying elements at 15 sampling locations in the WM taken at different heights. Five equally spaced depths along the weld thickness were selected, and at each depth three positions were sampled from left to right across the weld. The resulting compositions were plotted on a Schaeffler diagram to predict the phase constitution of the weld microstructure. The alloy content exhibits significant variations across different positions, with a notable concentration of Fe content observed in the lower portion of the weld. This variation can be attributed to the substantial compositional differences in Ni and Cr between the two BMs. Furthermore, the point EDS results suggest a weak through-thickness compositional tendency in the weld metal, where Fe appears relatively higher toward the lower region, while Ni and Cr show only a weak tendency to be relatively higher toward the upper region. Such variations are likely associated with convection-driven melt flow and local dilution differences during keyhole laser welding, although the through-thickness differences in Ni and Cr are relatively small in the present point EDS dataset. Fig. 3 Distribution diagram of primary elements in the WM and Schaeffler diagram for predicting weld microstructure:  a  Fe, Cr, and Ni concentrations measured at various locations using EPMA,  b  the position of the WM on the Schaeffer diagram

In accordance with the chemical composition presented in the table, and by substituting into Eqs. ( 1 ) and ( 2 ), the Ni equivalent and Cr equivalent were calculated, where the Cr equivalent is 15.8% and the Ni equivalent is 12.1%. As illustrated in Fig.  3 b, the Schaeffler diagram provides a semi-quantitative reference for identifying the WM microstructure as comprising of austenite and martensite.

Figure  4  shows the microstructural characteristics of the WM and the HAZ in the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint. As illustrated in Fig.  4 a, b, the WM on both the CLF-1 steel side and the 316LN-IG stainless steel side is predominantly constituted by lath martensite (LM) and columnar austenite (CA). The apparent equiaxed austenite grains should be interpreted as cross-sections perpendicular to the growth direction of the columnar austenite grains. Typical austenitic columnar grain epitaxial growth occurs in the WM near the 316LN-IG BM. Figure  4 c reveals distinct morphological differences on both sides of the WM. As demonstrated in previous studies [ 27 ], this phenomenon can be attributed to substantial variations in temperature gradients and solidification rates at the solidification fronts on either side of the molten pool. Fig. 4 SEM microstructures and compositional analysis of WM and HAZ of CLF-1/316LN-IG laser welded joint:  a  SEM micrograph of the WM on the CLF-1 side, showing lath martensite (LM) and columnar austenite (CA) dendrites. EDS line-scan path used to analyze the compositions of dendrites,  b  SEM micrograph of the WM on the 316LN-IG side, also exhibiting LM and CA dendrites. EDS line-scan path used to analyze the compositions of dendrites,  c  microstructure across the WM between the CLF-1 side and the 316LN-IG side,  d  overview of the CLF-1 side from the BM through the HAZ to the WM, the HAZ comprises CGHAZ, FGHAZ and ICHAZ,  e  microstructure across the fusion line between the WM and the 316LN-IG BM

Figure  4 d shows the HAZ on the CLF-1 steel side of the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint. The total width of the HAZ is approximately 300 μm and can be divided into several distinct regions based on thermal cycling characteristics. Among these, the region immediately adjacent to the fusion line constitutes the coarse-grained heat-affected zone (CGHAZ), located near the fusion line with a width of approximately 50 μm, as depicted in Fig.  4 d 1 . The microstructure in this sub-zone exhibits a coarser lath martensite morphology. Figure  4 d 2  displays the microstructural characteristics of the fine-grained heat-affected zone (FGHAZ) on the CLF-1 steel side within the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint. Compared with the CGHAZ, the FGHAZ region also presents a LM morphology, but with a finer and more uniform distribution. Figure  4 d 3  illustrates the microstructural characteristics of the intercritical heat-affected zone (ICHAZ) on the CLF-1 steel side of the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint. In this region, a mixture of tempered martensite, which is composed of equiaxed ferrite and fine-grained carbides, and fresh martensite was formed. Figure  4 e shows the microstructural characteristics of the fusion line on the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side of the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint. The austenitic structure persists in the proximity of the fusion line, and no distinct HAZ is observed on the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side.

sections.heading: EBSD analysis
paragraphs: As demonstrated in Fig.  5 , EBSD cross-section characterization was conducted on the CLF-1/316LN-IG dissimilar steels weld joint. No typical HAZ features were observed at the 316LN-IG-BM/WM interface (Fig.  5 a), whereas the CLF-1 BM/WM interface (Fig.  5 b) clearly exhibited CGHAZ, FGHAZ, and ICHAZ, consistent with SEM observations. Fig. 5 EBSD characterization of the CLF-1/316LN-IG dissimilar steels welded joint:  a  interface between 316LN-IG BM and the WM,  b  interface between CLF-1 BM and the WM, including the HAZ,  c–e  the WM of CLF-1 steel side:  c  inverse pole figure (IPF-Z) map,  d  kernel average misorientation (KAM) map,  e  misorientation angle distribution,  f–h  the WM of 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side:  f  IPF-Z map,  g  KAM map,  h  misorientation angle distribution

Figure  5 c, d, f, and g show that the WM on both sides consists of austenite and lath martensite, as revealed by IPF-Z and KAM maps. In the WM near the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side, austenite forms a continuous columnar dendritic network, whereas martensite appears as discrete islands. In contrast, in the WM near the CLF-1 steel side, martensite is matrix-dominant with thin lamellar austenite entrained within the matrix. The overall KAM distributions on both sides are at similar levels, qualitatively reflecting comparable local orientation gradients associated with geometrically necessary dislocations. Misorientation angle distribution maps (Fig.  5 e, h) reveal pronounced misorientations in the WM on both sides at low angles (< 10°), at approximately 45°, and at angles exceeding 50°. The low-angle misorientations are attributed to low-angle boundaries formed by the high dislocation density within lath martensite. Misorientation angle near 45° primarily reflects the orientation relationships across the austenite–martensite phase interface, notably the Kurdjumov–Sachs (K–S) and Nishiyama–Wassermann (N–W) orientation relationships. The K–S orientation relationship corresponds to a misorientation angle of 42.8°, whereas the N–W orientation relationship corresponds to 45.9° [ 32 ]. Furthermore, the proportion that conforms to the K–S orientation relationship in the WM near the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side is significantly higher than that on the CLF-1 steel side. This difference arises primarily from Ni/Cr dilution and solidification segregation, which increase austenite stability on the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side and promote the formation of a more continuous columnar austenite dendritic network. As a result, the number and length fraction of austenite–martensite phase interfaces increase statistically, thereby elevating the relative fraction of K–S orientations. Misorientation angles exceeding 50° closely match the canonical high-angle set associated with K–S variants, indicating that the hierarchical interfaces of the lath-martensite microstructure (lath, block, and packet boundaries) occupy a substantial fraction of the WM on both sides [ 33 ,  34 ]. The lath-martensite hierarchy interface is more fully developed on the CLF-1 steel side, resulting in a more pronounced K–S variant peak corresponding a misorientation angles exceeding 50°.

sections.heading: TEM analysis
paragraphs: Figure  6  presents the microstructural characterization results of the WM in the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint obtained via TEM. As shown in Fig.  6 a, the bright-field (BF) image clearly reveals lath structures within the WM region with a width of approximately 390 nm. Preliminary analysis identifies these structures as the LM phase. The selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern in Fig.  6 b shows α-Fe diffraction spots along the [110] crystal axis in region A, confirming the presence of lath martensite. Furthermore, Fig.  6 c reveals extensive dislocation structures (indicated by red arrows) within the lath martensite phase alongside relatively well-defined grain boundary features. Another set of BF images, shown in Fig.  6 d, reveals distinct austenitic structures within the WM region. This finding is consistent with the SEM analysis and the predicted results from the Schaeffler diagram. Subsequently, SAED analysis of region B (Fig.  6 e) reveals γ-Fe diffraction spots along the [100] crystal axis, confirming the austenite phase's presence in this region. Relatively long dislocation lines are also identified within the austenite (Fig.  6 f). A comprehensive analysis indicates that both the austenite and martensite phases coexist in the WM. Fig. 6 TEM characterization of the WM in the CLF-1/316LN-IG dissimilar steels welded joint:  a  BF-TEM image showing α-Fe,  b  SAED pattern from region A in ( a ),  c  magnified view of ( a ) highlighting the dislocation substructure within the α-Fe,  d  BF-TEM image showing γ-Fe,  e  SAED pattern from region B in ( d ),  f  magnified view of ( d ) highlighting the dislocation substructure within the γ-Fe

sections.heading: Microhardness
paragraphs: As shown in Fig.  9 , the microhardness distribution in the middle section of the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint exhibits the characteristic sub-zones of BM, WM, and HAZ. The microhardness distribution in the 316LN-IG BM region is uniform, with an average hardness of 217.2 HV 0.3 . The WM exhibits an average hardness of 340.0 HV 0.3 , which is significantly higher than that of the BM. This reflects the synergistic strengthening due to the formation of lath martensite and dense dislocation substructures formed during rapid cooling process in the WM. However, its hardness exhibits significant fluctuations, ranging from ~259.3 HV 0.3  to ~414.8 HV 0.3 . The peak hardness was observed in CGHAZ, reaching 523.7 HV 0.3 . This is attributed to complete austenitization and prior austenite grain coarsening due to the high peak temperature, followed by rapid cooling that retained untempered lath martensite and accumulated high-density dislocations, leading to strengthening. Due to lower peak temperatures, the FGHAZ and ICHAZ undergo only partial phase transformation accompanied by mild tempering. Although their hardness values are lower than those of the CGHAZ, they are still significantly higher than the WM, at approximately 410.2 HV 0.3  and 336.4 HV 0.3 , respectively. The CLF-1 BM region, away from the molten pool and less affected by welding thermal cycling, exhibits a more uniform hardness distribution with an average hardness of 196.4 HV 0.3 . Fig. 9 Microhardness distribution across the middle section of CLF-1/316LN-IG laser welded joints, including the 316LN-IG BM, WM, HAZ of CLF-1 and CLF-1 BM

sections.heading: Tensile properties
paragraphs: Figure  10  shows the tensile test results for the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded specimen, the CLF-1 BM, and 316LN-IG BM at room temperature. The tensile fracture specimens reveal that the fracture of the CLF-1/316LN-IG welded specimen occurred in the 316LN-IG BM, far from the WM, confirming that the welded region is not a weak point in the welded joint. Engineering stress–strain curves confirm that the welded joint has a yield strength markedly higher than that of the 316LN-IG BM and an ultimate tensile strength comparable to that of the 316LN-IG BM and approaching that of CLF-1 BM. However, the elongation of the welded specimens is markedly lower than that of the 316LN-IG BM, indicating reduced ductility. Table  4  summarizes the mean and standard deviation of the tensile properties of the CLF-1 BM, the 316LN-IG BM, and the CLF-1/316LN-IG laser welded specimens. Fig. 10 Tensile test results for the CLF-1/316LN-IG laser welded specimens, the CLF-1 BM, and 316LN-IG BM at room temperature: stress–strain curves and tensile fracture specimen images Table 4 Detailed tensile properties of CLF-1 BM, 316LN-IG BM and CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded specimens CLF-1 316LN-IG Welded joints Yield strength (MPa) 529.2 ± 1.9 328.2 ± 0.2 365.8 ± 5.0 Ultimate tensile strength (MPa) 669.8 ± 1.3 619.5 ± 0.4 619.0 ± 0.7 Total elongation (%) 26.7 ± 0.9 74.2 ± 1.0 45.5 ± 1.4 Uniform elongation (%) 7.1 ± 0.1 50.8 ± 2.9 23.8 ± 2.1

Figure  11  displays the macroscopic and SEM fracture morphologies of tensile specimens from the CLF-1 BM, 316LN-IG BM, and CLF-1/316LN-IG laser welded joints. In Fig.  11 a, the macro fracture of the CLF-1 BM reveals tear cracks propagating outward from the central fracture zone, indicating limited ductility. The corresponding SEM fracture image reveals predominantly intergranular ductile dimple tearing accompanied by cleavage faces and tear ridges, indicating a mixed fracture mode involving ductile and brittle fracture mechanisms. Figure  11 b shows the 316LN-IG BM specimen exhibiting significant necking without tearing. The SEM fracture surface displays equiaxed dimples only, indicating a ductile fracture mechanism dominated by micro-pore nucleation, growth, and coalescence. Figure  11 c shows continuous tearing ridges at the fracture center. SEM micrographs reveal a dense distribution of tear ridges in the central region, accompanied primarily by equiaxed dimples. Fig. 11 Macroscopic and SEM fracture morphologies of tensile specimens from the laser welded joints:  a  CLF-1 BM,  b  316LN-IG BM,  c  CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded conventional tensile specimens,  d  CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded notched tensile specimen

Since no significant failure occurred in the WM during conventional tensile testing, a V-notched tensile specimen was employed to evaluate the weld strength. The notch tip was meticulously positioned within the WM (geometric schematic shown in Fig.  1 b), thereby ensuring that crack nucleation and final fracture occurred in the weld rather than transferring to the BM.

Figure  11 d shows the SEM image of the fracture surface of the V-notch specimen, revealing predominantly fine, dense, equiaxed dimples. This pattern is consistent with the micro-pore aggregation characteristic of high-strength, low-toughness materials under high-constraint stress conditions. This result corresponds with the relatively higher load-bearing capacity of the WM and confirms the joint's strength advantage through fracture morphology.

sections.heading: Charpy impact properties
paragraphs: Figure  12  and Table  5  show the Charpy V-notch impact toughness results at room temperature for the CLF-1 BM, 316LN-IG BM, and CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint. The average absorbed impact energy was approximately 222.3 J for the CLF-1 BM, for the 316LN-IG BM approximately 336.7 J and for the CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joint approximately 239.7 J. The impact absorbed energy of the welded joint is intermediate between those of the CLF-1 and 316LN-IG BM. Fig. 12 Charpy V-notch impact toughness results at room temperature for the CLF-1 BM, 316LN-IG BM, and CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joints Table 5 Impact absorbed energy of CLF-1 BM, 316LN-IG BM and CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joints CLF-1 316LN-IG Welded joints Impact absorbed energy (J) 222.3 ± 9.6 336.7 ± 4.6 239.7 ± 15.9

Figure  13  shows the macroscopic and SEM fracture morphologies of impact specimens from the CLF-1 BM, 316LN-IG BM, and CLF-1/316LN-IG steels laser welded joints. In Fig.  13 a, the impact fracture morphology of the CLF-1 BM is dominated by ductile dimple tearing, with localized quasi-detachment steps and riverpatterns. Figure  13 b reveals that the impact fracture morphology of the 316LN-IG BM exhibits parabolically distributed ductile dimples. This is attributed to the intense shear and tensile deformation of micro-pores under impact loading and high-strain-rate plastic deformation conditions, representing typical ductile fracture. In Fig.  13 c, the fracture surface of the welded joint impact specimen exhibits a c1 region composed of large ductile dimples and continuous tear ridges, while the c2 region shows small ductile dimples with tear ridges exhibiting slight tensile orientation. Overall, both regions display a mixed fracture behavior dominated by ductile fracture with brittle contribution. sections.heading: Microstructural evolution of the dissimilar steels welded joint
paragraphs: Figures  4 – 8  summarize the multiscale microstructural characteristics of the CLF-1/316LN-IG laser-welded joints. SEM and EBSD reveal the morphology and crystallographic features of the WM and the subdivided CLF-1 HAZ (Figs.  4 ,  5 ), while TEM identifies the α-Fe and γ-Fe phases in the WM and the TaC and (Cr, W) 23 C 6  precipitates in the CLF-1 HAZ together with their orientation relationships with the martensitic matrix (Figs.  6 – 8 ). These observations collectively indicate that the microstructural heterogeneity of the dissimilar joint is strongly governed by the welding thermal cycle and the distinct phase transformation responses of the two base metals.

The formation of different HAZ sub-regions on the CLF-1 side is mainly determined by the thermal cycling temperature. In the CGHAZ, the peak temperature significantly exceeds A c 3 . The original tempered martensite structure of the base metal undergoes complete austenitization during the high-temperature welding thermal cycle and transforms into lath martensite upon cooling. The proximity of this region to the fusion line exposes the material to elevated temperatures, thereby increasing the driving force for grain growth and producing pronounced austenite coarsening, which ultimately leads to the formation of the CGHAZ. In contrast to the CGHAZ, the FGHAZ also undergoes complete austenitization as its peak temperature exceeds A c 3 . However, due to a slightly lower temperature and shorter high-temperature dwell time, grain growth is not significant. Upon the cooling process, it transforms into a lath martensite structure with a finer grain size and a more uniform distribution. As the distance from the fusion line increases further, the peak temperature of the HAZ decreases to between A c 1  and A c 3 , forming the ICHAZ. In this region, the welding thermal cycling temperature is lower, thereby preventing complete austenitization of the BM. Consequently, a mixed microstructure is formed, consisting of tempered martensite, which is composed of equiaxed ferrite and fine-grained carbides, and fresh martensite was formed. On the 316LN-IG side, although the 316LN-IG BM adjacent to the fusion line exceeds the austenitizing temperature during laser welding, 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel is a typical stable austenitic stainless steel. The austenitic structure persists in the proximity of the fusion line without undergoing solid-state phase transformation, and no distinct HAZ is observed on the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side under the present metallographic observations. This contrast between the two sides highlights that the dominant microstructural evolution of the joint is controlled by the martensitic transformation behavior of the RAFM steel and the thermal stability of the austenitic stainless steel.

The formation of columnar dendritic austenite in WM is attributed to the combined effects of composition, undercooling, and epitaxial growth. SEM results and EBSD analyses (Figs.  4 ,  5 ) demonstrate that there is orientation continuity across fusion lines and axial grain elongation along heat flow directions, indicating that the newly formed solid phase epitaxially grows into the molten pool using the parent γ-Fe as a template. The molten pool cools along the γ-Fe primary solidification path on the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side. Solute redistribution occurs at the leading edge of the liquid–solid interface: Ni and Mn enrich within columnar dendrites, while Cr and Mo enrich in dendrite interstices, as confirmed by the EDS line scans in Fig.  4 a, b. This shifts the local liquidus temperature downwards, inducing composition undercooling and thereby destabilizing the planar interface and initiating dendritic growth. The high temperature gradient and growth rate ratio during welding provide stable boundary conditions for directional epitaxy, enabling dendrite tips to continuously propagate along the heat flow normal direction. These dendrites extend from the fusion line into the molten pool and freeze during cooling and solidification, ultimately forming a weld microstructure dominated by columnar austenitic dendrites.

In the inter-dendritic regions, the concentrations of Ni and Mn are relatively low. Concurrently, the high cooling rate during welding increases the  Ms , as calculated by Eq. ( 4 ). This causes the undercooled austenite to undergo a non-diffusive phase transformation. According to Eq. ( 4 ), the enrichment of Cr and Ni in dendrite cores causes a pronounced decrease in  Ms , favoring the retention of austenite. Conversely, the inter-dendritic region exhibits a lower overall content of Ni and Mn, resulting in a relatively elevated  Ms , and allowing for a higher martensite volume fraction at the final cooling temperature (Eq.  3 ), forming the characteristic microstructure of lath martensite embedded within a columnar austenite matrix.

Under the conditions of low heat input and rapid cooling of laser welding, the formation of TaC and (Cr, W) 23 C 6  phases in the HAZ on the CLF-1 steel side follows a dissolution, redistribution, and reprecipitation sequence. At peak temperature, the equilibrium solubility of fine particles is higher, which causes the original M 23 C 6  phase to dissolve preferentially. In contrast, the MX phase, which has a higher dissolution temperature, only partially dissolves and persists as potential nucleation sites for subsequent reprecipitation [ 41 ,  42 ]. As the temperature decreases, the solubility of interstitial elements such as C and N in the matrix decreases rapidly, producing supersaturation and enrichment near lath boundaries via bulk diffusion [ 43 ] Conversely, substitutional elements such as Cr, W, and Ta migrate predominantly along short-circuit pathways such as dislocations and grain boundaries [ 44 ], resulting in new phases nucleate and grow preferentially at these defect-rich sites. This mechanism results in the diffuse precipitation of the TaC phase within and near lath boundaries (Fig.  7 ), while discrete M 23 C 6  phases form along grain boundaries (Fig.  8 ).

sections.heading: Phase stability of TaC and (Cr, W) 23 C 6  in HAZ
paragraphs: Based on TEM-EDS analysis, both types of precipitates in the HAZ of this study were identified as carbides. However, the BM also contains metallic elements such as Fe, Mn, and V, which theoretically could also participate in the formation of MX and M 23 C 6  phases. To further clarify the stability of these candidate carbides and to provide a basis for subsequent phase stability and alloy design, DFT calculations are employed to systematically evaluate the formation enthalpies and elastic moduli of representative MX (TaC, VC) and M 23 C 6  (Fe 23 C 6 , Cr 23 C 6 , Mn 23 C 6 ) phases. It should be noted that the DFT calculations were performed on idealized periodic crystal models and are used here to provide a comparative stability ranking of candidate carbide phases.

To qualitatively analyze the contribution of precipitates to mechanical behavior, we employ the bulk modulus (B) and shear modulus (G), which were obtained from DFT calculations, to evaluate the brittle-ductile tendency of the phases. According to the Pugh criterion, B/G = 1.75 is the brittle-ductile threshold, B/G < 1.75 indicates a brittle phase, while B/G > 1.75 indicates a ductile phase [ 49 ]. As shown in Table S2, the calculation results indicate that TaC has a B value of 333.8 GPa and a G value of 200.8 GPa, with B/G equal to 1.66. Therefore, TaC belongs to the brittle phase. In the M 23 C 6  system, the metal lattice contains inequivalent sites (4a, 8c, 32f, 48h), and W substitution exhibits site preference and elemental disorder. In the absence of site occupancy statistics, a single (Cr, W) 23 C 6  model is not representative. Therefore, we first adopt the DFT-computed properties of Cr 23 C 6  as a baseline (B = 510.9 GPa, G = 159.3 GPa, B/G = 1.93, classified as ductile) and compare them with a limited set of published (Cr, W) 23 C 6  calculations. According to the literature [ 47 ], the B/G range for (Cr, W) 23 C 6  is 2.03–2.11, which also exceeds the Pugh threshold of 1.75 and therefore indicates a ductile character, which is consistent with the B/G determination results for Cr 23 C 6  in this study. TaC predominantly acts as dispersed intralath particles that pin dislocations and provide strengthening, whereas discrete (Cr, W) 23 C 6  precipitates along grain boundaries provide boundary pinning and impede boundary migration. Together, these precipitates determine the balance between strength and toughness in the HAZ.

sections.heading: Comprehensive analysis of microstructure and mechanical property relationships
paragraphs: The mechanical properties of the laser welded joints were comprehensively evaluated through hardness (Fig.  9 ), tensile (Figs.  10 ,  11 ), and Charpy impact tests (Figs.  12 ,  13 ), with the results compared to the BMs on both sides.

The engineering stress–strain curve indicates that the welded joint exhibits tensile strength comparable to the 316LN-IG BM, with significantly enhanced yield strength (YS) and higher elongation than the CLF-1 BM. This combination of strength and ductility is consistent with the joint's multiscale microstructure. Within the WM, lath martensite is embedded in a columnar austenite matrix. The martensite phase is characterized by a high density of dislocations and interfaces, while the presence of columnar austenite dendrites contributes to the manifestation of plasticity. Additionally, uniformly dispersed MX-type TaC precipitates within the HAZ act as stable dislocation barriers, forcing dislocations to bypass the precipitates during movement. HRTEM images of the TaC-matrix interface (Fig.  7 a) reveal dislocation arrays and lattice edge bending around TaC particles, indicating that moving dislocations become pinned and pile up at such precipitates. Furthermore, (Cr, W) 23 C 6  carbides decorating the grain boundaries were observed in the CLF-1 HAZ, exhibiting a distinct orientation relationship with the α-Fe matrix (Fig.  8 f). Therefore, the synergistic interaction between the diffusely distributed TaC and the (Cr, W) 23 C 6  barrier at grain boundaries in the HAZ increases the critical stress required for dislocation bypassing, thereby significantly enhancing YS [ 50 ]. Tensile fracture morphology (Fig.  10 ) reveals that although both the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel specimens and welded specimens fractured in the 316LN-IG region, the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel specimen exhibited typical uniform ductile fracture (Fig.  11 b), while the weld specimen exhibited shallower dimples and distinct tear ridges (Fig.  11 c). This different indicates that the high-hardness martensite in the WM and CLF-1 HAZ exacerbated stress concentration and strain localization on the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side. During the uniform deformation stage, plastic strain is preferentially accommodated by the softer 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side due to yield strength mismatch, thereby limiting the overall work hardening and ultimate load-bearing capacity of the joint. Given the spatial variation across the fracture surface, the superior ductility of 316LN-IG dominates deformation compatibility at the early stage of tensile straining, leading to the formation of relatively small and equiaxed dimples in the edge region (Fig.  11 c2). The fracture morphology in this region is highly consistent with that of the 316LN-IG base metal (Fig.  11 b), indicating a ductile fracture mechanism primarily governed by the austenitic matrix. With further loading, the high-strength weld metal imposes geometric and mechanical constraints on the necking process in the 316LN-IG region, resulting in enhanced local strain concentration and accelerated damage evolution. Consequently, the central region of the fracture surface (Fig.  11 c1) transitions to a tearing-dominated morphology characterized by more pronounced tear ridges and relatively larger dimples, reflecting an unstable fracture process under constrained plastic deformation.

The impact absorbed energy of the welded joint is intermediate between those of CLF-1 steel and 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel. Fractography shows mixed quasi-cleavage and shallow dimples in the CLF-1 steel specimen, parabolic dimples in the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel specimen, and dimples with tear ridges in the welded joint specimen (Fig.  13 ). These features are indicative of the constrained state of the HAZ and its characteristics at the grain boundaries. The strength mismatch between the WM and BM, coupled with residual tensile stresses, elevates the triaxial stress at the notch and reduces the effective fracture resistance.

sections.heading: Feasibility and engineering applicability of welding CLF-1 steel with 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel
paragraphs: In this study, the primary structural materials of TBMs, namely CLF-1 steel and 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel, were dissimilarly joined by laser welding technology. A systematic assessment of the microstructure and mechanical properties indicates that the WM formed a dense and stable microstructure consisting of lath martensite and columnar austenitic dendrites. Two stable precipitate phases, TaC and (Cr, W) 23 C 6 , are present in the CLF-1-side HAZ. These microstructural features enable the weld to meet tensile strength and impact toughness levels comparable to those of 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel and CLF-1 steel, thereby demonstrating the feasibility and engineering applicability of laser welding for dissimilar joining of CLF-1 steel and 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel. Overall, the welded joint exhibits an acceptable equilibrium of strength and toughness between the two BMs. These results provide a clear baseline for the engineering application of dissimilar materials welded joints in critical TBM components fabrication, primarily in terms of the as-welded microstructure and room-temperature mechanical response, service-relevant performance, including high-temperature performance, irradiation effects, and long-term stability, requires further investigation.

To advance application expansion and service reliability, future work will conduct irradiation effect assessments by simulating real-service environments through ion irradiation. Compare irradiation damage behavior in the welded joints before and after irradiation to establish a mapping relationship between microstructure, damage behavior, and mechanical properties. This will define the operational window and service life limits for laser welded joints under extreme service conditions.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study systematically investigated the heterogeneous interfacial microstructure evolution and strengthening behavior of laser-welded CLF-1/316LN-IG dissimilar steel joints by integrating multiscale experimental characterization with first-principles and thermodynamic calculations. The following conclusions can be drawn: Defect-free CLF-1/316LN-IG dissimilar steel welded joints were successfully fabricated using laser welding. A well-developed HAZ was observed on the CLF-1 steel side, whereas no discernible HAZ was identified on the 316LN-IG side, which is attributed to the excellent high-temperature microstructural stability of austenitic stainless steel. The WM exhibited a heterogeneous microstructure consisting of lath martensite and columnar austenitic dendrites, arising from the rapid solidification and compositional redistribution during laser welding. In the WM near the 316LN-IG austenitic stainless steel side, austenite formed a continuous columnar dendritic network, whereas martensite appeared as discrete islands. In contrast, in the WM near the CLF-1 steel side, martensite was matrix-dominant with thin lamellar austenite entrained within the matrix. Intragranular TaC and intergranular (Cr, W) 23 C 6  carbides were identified in the CLF-1 HAZ by TEM characterization. First-principles calculations and thermodynamic analysis further revealed that TaC exhibits higher phase stability among MX-type carbides, while (Cr, W) 23 C 6  is the most stable phase among M 23 C 6 -type carbides. The calculated results are in good agreement with the experimental observations, providing a quantitative basis for understanding the precipitation sequence and phase stability in the HAZ. The CLF-1/316LN-IG welded joint exhibited good overall mechanical performance. The UTS reached 619.0 MPa, comparable to that of 316LN-IG steel. The YS was 365.8 MPa, 11.5% higher than that of 316LN-IG, and the total elongation reached 45.5%, 70.4% higher than that of CLF-1 steel. Tensile fracture occurred in the 316LN-IG base material region away from the weld. The Charpy impact toughness of the welded joint was between those of CLF-1 and 316LN-IG steels, demonstrating that the weld region was not the mechanical weak zone of the joint.
